name: USearch
baseline: FAISS (HNSW index build; exact brute-force search via faiss.IndexFlatL2)
workload: HNSW index construction time for 100 million vectors (96-dimensional and 1536-dimensional; f32, f16 and i8 storage) with inner-product distance on Intel Sapphire Rapids at equal recall and memory; plus an exact brute-force k-NN search example against faiss.IndexFlatL2 in Google Colab.
claimed_speedup: README: '10x faster HNSW implementation than FAISS'. Indexing time, 100 Million 96d f32/f16/i8 vectors: FAISS 2.6/2.6/2.6 h vs USearch 0.3/0.2/0.2 h (9.6/10.4/10.7x). 100 Million 1536d f32/f16/i8: FAISS 5.0/4.1/3.8 h vs USearch 2.1/1.1/0.8 h (2.3/3.6/4.4x). Exact search vs FAISS IndexFlatL2: 55.3 ms vs 2.54 ms ('up to a 20x performance improvement').
hardware: Intel Sapphire Rapids (exact CPU model, core count and RAM not stated in the README); the exact-search example ran on a Google Colab CPU instance (not further specified)
stars_or_usage: 4.3k stars; integrated by ClickHouse, DuckDB, YugabyteDB and others (per README)
tradeoffs: Single-header C++11 core with bindings for 10 languages, user-defined metrics with JIT, f16/bf16/i8 quantization, disk-viewed indexes and 40-bit IDs. Different defaults from FAISS (connectivity 16 vs 32, expansion at add 128 vs 40, expansion at search 64 vs 16, per BENCHMARKS.md), so recall/speed trade-offs are not identical to FAISS defaults.
caveats: First-party README numbers only: the linked benchmark blog (unum.cloud, 2023-11-07) was EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the setup behind the indexing-time table could not be checked, and the README gives no exact CPU model, thread count, compiler or flags (hence tier C). The 10x headline holds for 96d vectors; 1536d gains are 2.3-4.4x. The 55.3 ms vs 2.54 ms exact-search figures come from a comment on issue #176 that the README links that could not be opened; the issue's own original report (500 vectors x 1024d, k=50, Colab) measured USearch exact search at 94.7 ms vs FAISS IndexFlatL2 at 1.14 ms (labelled bug/invalid, later released), so the exact-search result is workload- and version-dependent. In-tree BENCHMARKS.md has USearch-only QPS tables (Graviton 3, c7g.metal) with no FAISS rows; python/scripts/bench_exact.py can run '--backend usearch,faiss' for reproduction. Category kept as autodiff-and-ml-kernels (FAISS sits there in the catalog); it is a vector-search/ANN library.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp#Machine Learning (listed as 'Fast search and clustering library for vectors and strings'), then the project's README, BENCHMARKS.md and python/scripts/bench_exact.py via raw.githubusercontent.com and github.com issue #176

name: XGBoost
baseline: scikit-learn GradientBoostingClassifier 0.15.2 and R gbm package (gradient-boosted trees training)
workload: Training time of gradient-boosted trees for binary classification (flight-delay prediction from the airline dataset, 10K to 10M rows, mostly categorical features, AUC measured on a 100K test set). Experiment A: 1000 trees, depth 16, learn rate 0.01, subsample 0.5. Experiment B: 300 trees, depth 6, learn rate 0.1.
claimed_speedup: Time in seconds, xgboost vs R gbm: 10K A 6 vs 20, B 1 vs 3; 100K A 40 vs 200, B 4 vs 30; 1M A 400 vs 3000 (7.5x, derived from page data), B 45 vs 400 (8.9x, derived from page data); R gbm has no 10M run in A, 10M B 5000 vs xgboost 1000. xgboost vs scikit-learn: 10K A 6 vs 1100 (about 183x, derived from page data), B 1 vs 120; 100K B 4 vs 1500 (375x, derived from page data); scikit-learn has no larger runs. AUC similar (e.g. 10K A 70.3 xgboost vs 69.9 scikit-learn vs 64.9 R; 1M A 76.9 xgboost vs 74.1 R).
hardware: Amazon EC2 c3.8xlarge (32 cores, 60 GB RAM); r3.8xlarge (32 cores, 250 GB RAM) for some larger runs. Ubuntu 14.04, R 3.2.0, scikit-learn 0.15.2, xgboost 0.4-0 (github snapshot 2015-05-16). CPU model and xgboost build flags not stated.
tradeoffs: Multithreaded exact/histogram tree boosting with sparse-aware data structures, distributed and GPU modes; the benchmark's xgboost run used a sparse one-hot matrix and nthread = detectCores(). Memory was 1 GB at 1M rows (6 GB at 10M in experiment A).
caveats: Independent third-party suite (szilard/benchm-ml, scripts 3-boosting/1-gbm.R, 2-boost.py, 6-xgboost.R) but the thread counts are not equal: xgboost used all 32 cores while the README calls R gbm 'a single-threaded implementation'. Hyperparameters are matched only approximately and the resulting models differ somewhat in AUC. Versions date from 2015 (xgboost 0.4, scikit-learn 0.15.2 before HistGradientBoostingClassifier existed); the benchmark's own 2017 update says LightGBM is now the fastest GBM tool, and sklearn only ran for 10K and 100K rows. XGBoost is itself the category incumbent, and the KDD 2016 paper (arXiv 1603.02754, 'more than ten times faster than existing solutions' vs scikit-learn/R gbm on Higgs) could not be opened here (arxiv.org, hyper.ai and uwaterloo mirrors EGRESS_BLOCKED), so its numbers are not recorded. The repo's demo/kaggle-higgs/speedtest.py compares xgboost with sklearn GBM but publishes no numbers (Python 2 era script). Category kept as autodiff-and-ml-kernels although the guessed baselines (tensorflow, pytorch) do not apply.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp#Machine Learning (listed as 'Scalable, Portable and Distributed Gradient Boosting Library'), then the dmlc/xgboost README (no numbers), demo/kaggle-higgs/speedtest.py and szilard/benchm-ml README (raw.githubusercontent.com)

name: Yeppp!
baseline: Julia Base log (pure-Julia Float64 implementation), measured through the Yeppp.jl binding
workload: Elementwise natural logarithm of an array of 10^7 random Float64 values: Yeppp.log!(similar(x), x) vs Base log(x), timed with @elapsed in the Yeppp.jl README example.
claimed_speedup: 3x ('Yeppp's vectorized log is 3x faster than the one in Base, which is written in Julia')
stars_or_usage: the Julia binding Yeppp.jl has 54 stars (archived 2020-04); no star count for the mirror
tradeoffs: Array-oriented SIMD library (vector add, multiply, dot, sum, log, exp, sin, cos, tan, polynomial evaluation) for 15 platforms across x86, ARM, PowerPC and MIPS, callable from C, C++, C#, Java and FORTRAN, with runtime dispatch to the best instruction set. Operates on whole arrays, not a drop-in scalar libm replacement.
caveats: The only number reachable is a one-line claim in the Yeppp.jl (Julia binding) README, a first-party-style example with no hardware, Julia version, compiler or flags, and the baseline is Julia's own log rather than glibc libm or Intel MKL. The official Bitbucket repository (bitbucket.org/MDukhan/yeppp) now returns 404, so repo_url is the unofficial GitHub mirror (last commit 2015-08-24; its README has no benchmarks). The project's own comparisons against MKL/libm on yeppp.info and docs.yeppp.info, the PPAM 2013 paper (Dukhan and Vuduc) and the Hot Chips 25 poster were EGRESS_BLOCKED and are not recorded. Category big-integer-arbitrary-precision (guessed from the list) is wrong; it is a vector math library, closest to math-simd-linear-algebra.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/oz123/awesome-c#Numerical (listed as 'Fast, SIMD-optimized mathematical library'), then the github.com/wdv4758h/Yeppp mirror README and the JuliaMath/Yeppp.jl README
